doc.title: Winard Harper interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 10, 2014

title: Changes in recording and the CD era
summary: Harper recalls being among the first bands on CD in the 80s and how the industry was unprepared for downloads.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Has the importance of making recordings changed?

Yeah there’s very few of them and nowadays for someone to record there’s not a whole lot you can do with them. Because, and that’s the other thing that happened. This hurt quite a bit. I think the industry wasn’t prepared either for where things were going. So you know it’s kind of like well we came on the scene in the 80s and we were one of the first bands to start going CDs. You know what I mean? That format.
Yeah. That was the time, yeah.

So I think when we came it was us and Wynton and Branford and Roy Hargrove came a little behind us, but we were some of the first, our first recording was album, CD and cassette. So now all that’s changed. But I don’t think the industry saw a lot of things coming. So now with the computer and the digital downloads and then one of the first things that hurt them, you know, Tower Records had come in, like in what was that in the late 70s, early 80s. And they killed all the Mom and Pop stores because they were such a big chain. You know it’s almost like WalMart. Nobody could compete. So a lot of your Mom and Pop stores went out then. Then when Tower failed there’s nothing really. So you know nobody was really prepared for all that. So I think even for record companies and stuff now, a lot of thought has to be given because there’s not a whole lot of places to sell records unless the musicians are selling them off the bandstand themselves. So doing CDs is a little trickier.

Oh you have to, hoping to get some airplay, keep your name out there. But the thing is it’s almost like you’re doing it and everybody almost kind of knows well if we sell X amount we’re lucky. You know what I mean?
Right. It’s not going to be a money maker.
